title: Vietnamese sounds and spelling
description: A guided 45–60 minute first lesson: understand Vietnamese syllables, vowel letters, tone marks and how to read carefully without using English spelling habits.
teacher_intro: Welcome to your first Northern Vietnamese lesson. Set aside about 45–60 minutes. You do not need to memorise everything immediately. The method is simple: listen to the teacher, think about the answer, say it aloud before the students answer, and only then compare. Today we are learning how Vietnamese writing works. We are not trying to master every sound or all six tones yet; those will be trained more carefully in later lessons. Keep a notebook nearby if you want, but speak first.
background: The modern Vietnamese writing system is chữ Quốc ngữ. It uses Latin letters, additional vowel letters and diacritics. A written space normally separates syllables. Several syllables can work together as one meaningful expression: học sinh means 'student' and giáo viên means 'teacher'. There are two different jobs that marks can do. First, vowel marks distinguish vowel letters such as a, ă and â; e and ê; o, ô and ơ; u and ư. Second, tone marks distinguish the six tones. For the vowel a, the written forms are a, á, à, ả, ã and ạ. Do not treat these marks as decoration. They are part of the spelling and meaning. This lesson introduces the system; detailed tone production and difficult vowel/consonant contrasts are practised in Lessons 2 and 3.
culture: Chữ Quốc ngữ became the standard writing system used in modern Vietnamese education and everyday life. Earlier Vietnamese writing included chữ Nôm, and classical Chinese characters were also used in formal contexts. Today, Vietnamese is normally written with Quốc ngữ. In this course, examples and pronunciation guidance follow contemporary Northern Vietnamese, with a Hanoi reference accent. Regional varieties are valid; the course simply uses one consistent model so that you can build a reliable foundation.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Before we begin, remember the method. I will give you a small piece of information, then ask you to build something. Pause the lesson if you need more time. Say your answer aloud before you reveal or read the student's answer.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So I should not just read the Vietnamese after you. I should try to produce it first.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Your attempt is the important part. A mistake is useful because it shows us what needs adjusting.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: First idea: Vietnamese is organised into syllables. A syllable is a spoken beat. A written space usually marks the boundary between syllables.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Does that mean every space separates a completely separate idea?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. A phrase or compound meaning may contain several syllables. Look at học sinh. It means 'student', but it is written as two syllables: học and sinh.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Your turn. If I give you the English meaning 'student', what two-syllable Vietnamese expression have we just learned? Pause and say it.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Học sinh.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Keep the two syllables distinct. Do not squash them into one English-style syllable.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now build another one. Giáo viên means 'teacher'. Listen to the two parts: giáo… viên. Say the complete expression.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Giáo viên.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Notice that the written space is still there. When you read Vietnamese, give each syllable its own clear shape.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's test the idea. 'Vietnamese language' is tiếng Việt. How many written syllables can you see? Count them before answering.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Two: tiếng and Việt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. The written space helps you see the two syllables.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A useful habit: when you meet a new expression, first identify the syllable boundaries. Then look at the consonants and vowel. Finally, notice the tone mark. Do not guess from the English translation.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should look at the whole written syllable, not just the first letter.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now we need to understand the marks above and below the letters.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Vietnamese uses familiar Latin letters, but some vowels have their own written forms. For example, a, ă and â are three distinct vowel letters. The small marks are not optional styling.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: If I leave off the mark, am I still writing the same vowel?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. The vowel identity changes. We will practise the exact mouth positions in Lesson 3. For now, train your eyes to recognise that a, ă and â are different letters.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: There are other groups too: e and ê; o, ô and ơ; u and ư. You do not need to master their pronunciation today. Just learn to see each spelling accurately.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I can see that o, ô and ơ are not interchangeable.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Right. A useful reading routine is: identify the vowel letter exactly as written, including its mark. Never silently remove a diacritic.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now we come to a second job performed by marks: tone. Vietnamese has six tone categories in the standard teaching description. We will study how to hear and produce them in Lesson 2.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For now, look at the six written forms built on a: a, á, à, ả, ã, ạ. The unmarked form is one tone; each of the five marked forms represents another tone category.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So the accent marks are not just telling me which vowel to use. They can also tell me the tone.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Be careful not to confuse a vowel mark with a tone mark. In ă, the breve changes the vowel letter. In á, the acute accent marks the tone on the vowel a.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: And ắ would combine the changed vowel with a tone mark?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. A Vietnamese syllable can show both a vowel-shape mark and a tone mark. That is why careful spelling matters.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's apply the routine to a familiar expression. Cảm ơn means 'thank you'. It has two written syllables. Look at the marks: cảm has a hỏi tone mark; ơn has the special vowel ơ.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So I should not write it as cam on without the marks.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. That would remove important spelling information. Write the complete forms, including the marks.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now try tiếng Việt. Both syllables carry tone marks. Read the spelling carefully from left to right, keeping the two syllables separate.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. You are learning to notice the information before you speak.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's review the three-step reading routine. One: find the syllable boundaries. Two: identify the exact vowel letters and their marks. Three: identify the tone mark. Only then produce the sound.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Syllables, vowel spelling, tone marks.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now we will build short expressions from English prompts. Do not rush. Give yourself several seconds before checking the answer.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Prompt one: 'student'. Think of the two syllables we learned. Say the Vietnamese expression now.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Học sinh.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Prompt two: 'teacher'. Build it from giáo and viên.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Giáo viên.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Prompt three: 'Vietnamese language'. Keep both syllables and their marks.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Prompt four: 'thank you'. Notice the vowel ơ in the second syllable and the tone mark in the first.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Cảm ơn.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now combine what you know. 'Vietnamese student' is học sinh Việt Nam. Count the syllables: học, sinh, Việt, Nam. Four clear syllables.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Học sinh Việt Nam.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Do not turn this into one long blur. Keep the syllables clear and connected naturally.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A short cultural note: the writing system you are learning is chữ Quốc ngữ. It is the everyday writing system used in modern Vietnam. You will see it in signs, messages, books, menus and official documents.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: And older Vietnamese writing included chữ Nôm?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Chữ Nôm was used historically, alongside classical Chinese characters in some formal settings. Modern everyday Vietnamese is written in Quốc ngữ.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Before we finish, let's do a listening-and-noticing routine with a native Northern Vietnamese speaker. First listen without repeating. Then listen again and repeat one syllable at a time. Finally listen at natural speed.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — careful pace: học… sinh. Pause. giáo… viên. Pause. tiếng… Việt. Pause. cảm… ơn. Pause. học… sinh… Việt… Nam.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — natural pace: học sinh; giáo viên; tiếng Việt; cảm ơn; học sinh Việt Nam. Keep the syllables clear and use natural connected speech.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now repeat the same set without looking at the written answers. If one expression is difficult, return to its individual syllables and build it again.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I can see that the marks are part of the word, and the spaces help me divide the syllables.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is the foundation. You do not need perfect pronunciation yet. Today you have learned how to read the written structure carefully. In Lesson 2, we will train the six Northern Vietnamese tones. In Lesson 3, we will work on vowel contrasts and difficult consonants.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Final challenge: explain the three steps to yourself, then say học sinh, giáo viên, tiếng Việt, cảm ơn and học sinh Việt Nam without looking. Take your time. When you can do that, mark the lesson complete.

title: The six tones
description: Distinguish the six Northern Vietnamese tones and hear why tone changes meaning.
teacher_intro: Today we train your ear and voice to distinguish all six Vietnamese tones, using a contemporary Hanoi/Northern model. We begin with the controlled syllable ma so the consonant and vowel stay familiar while the tone changes. Work slowly: listen, think, speak, then compare. Do not shout, strain your throat, or exaggerate the pitch.
background: Vietnamese is a tonal language: tone is part of a syllable's identity. The six tones are ngang (level, unmarked), sắc (rising, acute accent), huyền (falling, grave accent), hỏi (often dipping, hook-shaped mark), ngã (often creaky or interrupted and rising in Northern speech, tilde), and nặng (short, low and constricted, dot below). These are useful teaching descriptions, not rigid musical notes. Real pitch contours vary with speaker, voice range, sentence position and intonation. The familiar ma/má/mà/mả/mã/mạ set is a tone demonstration, not a claim that all six forms are equally common everyday vocabulary items.
culture: This course models contemporary Hanoi/Northern pronunciation. Northern and Southern varieties differ in the realisation of some tones and consonants; neither is inherently more correct. In Northern speech, the ngã tone often has a more noticeable glottal or creaky interruption than in some Southern varieties. Listen to several native speakers over time, because individuals and speaking styles vary.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Today we are going to make the six tones feel like six different movements of the voice. We will not rush. First listen, then think, then speak.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I know that Vietnamese uses marks above or below the vowel. Are those marks the tones?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: They are tone marks, but remember that the tone is part of the spoken syllable. The mark is a useful spelling clue; your ear and voice must learn the sound.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should not just read the letters and guess?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Read the syllable, notice its mark, recall the sound movement, and say the whole syllable as one unit.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Our demonstration syllable is ma. It lets us keep the consonant and vowel almost constant while we practise changing the tone.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — say ma three times with a relaxed, level pitch. Pause. The recording itself has not yet been supplied.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The first tone is ngang, the level tone. Keep the pitch steady and the voice relaxed. Do not make it flat by becoming quiet or breathless.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can keep the pitch level, but I tend to make the syllable sound like a question.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a common habit from English. Let the pitch stay even rather than rising at the end.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Does ngang have a tone mark?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No separate tone mark is written for ngang. The absence of a tone mark is meaningful: it represents the level tone.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now the second tone: sắc. Its pitch rises. Begin comfortably and move upward through the vowel. Do not confuse rising pitch with shouting.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — ma, then má. Leave a short silence between the two so the contrast is easy to hear.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I hear the second one lift. Should I make it much louder?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. Keep roughly the same comfortable volume. Change the pitch movement, not the force.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: And the acute accent is the mark for sắc?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. In má, the acute accent marks the rising tone.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The third tone is huyền, the falling tone. Let the pitch move downward smoothly. Keep the vowel clear until it finishes.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So sắc rises and huyền falls?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Practise them as opposite movements: má rises; mà falls.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — má, mà; repeat each twice at a slow teaching pace, then once naturally.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I sometimes hear a falling tone as if the speaker is tired.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That impression may help at first, but do not act out an emotion. Huyền is a linguistic tone, not a signal that the speaker feels sad or tired.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The fourth tone is hỏi. For many Hanoi speakers it has a low dipping movement: the pitch falls and then turns upward. The exact contour varies with context.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Is it like making a small curve rather than a straight fall?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a useful starting image. Listen carefully to a Northern model and imitate the whole movement without exaggerating it.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: The mark is a little hook, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. The hỏi mark is written above the vowel and is a reminder to learn this distinctive tone.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — say mả slowly, hold the vowel naturally, and repeat it in a short sequence with mà. No audio file is attached yet.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The fifth tone is ngã. In Northern speech it often has a noticeable interruption or creaky quality before the pitch rises.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: That sounds more interrupted than hỏi.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good observation. Do not simply make a second syllable or insert a strong pause. The interruption belongs inside one syllable.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Is the tilde the mark for ngã?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. The tilde appears above the vowel in mã.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The sixth tone is nặng. It is typically short, low and constricted in Northern speech. Finish it cleanly; do not add an extra vowel after it.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So it is not just a low version of huyền?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Right. Huyền is usually a smoother falling tone. Nặng is shorter and has a tighter, heavier ending.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: The dot is underneath the vowel for nặng?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. The dot below is the tone mark for nặng.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — contrast mà and mạ, then mã and mạ. Keep the syllables short and clear.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us put all six in order: ma, má, mà, mả, mã, mạ. First listen to the sequence without repeating.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can recognise the rising and falling ones more easily than the last three.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is normal. Give hỏi, ngã and nặng extra listening time. Their details are especially important in a Northern accent.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Can I practise the tones separately before using real words?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Begin with controlled syllables, then move quickly into useful vocabulary. Never assume the demonstration syllable is a complete vocabulary lesson.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A traditional teaching set uses ma with six different tone marks. It is a sound demonstration. The written forms do not all have equally common everyday meanings.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So I should remember the sound contrast, not memorise six translations for ma?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Learn vocabulary as complete words in context, with their tone.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now compare ngang and sắc: ma, má. Keep the vowel length similar and change only the tone.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Ma is level; má rises.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now compare sắc and huyền: má, mà. Make the direction clear.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Má rises; mà falls.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now compare hỏi and ngã. Both can have a turning movement, but ngã in Northern speech often has a creaky interruption.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I should listen for the voice quality as well as the pitch.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Precisely. A pitch sketch alone cannot teach every detail of a real voice.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now compare ngã and nặng. Keep mã as one interrupted syllable with a rise; make mạ short, low and constricted.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can feel that mạ finishes more abruptly.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a helpful physical cue. Keep it natural rather than forcing your throat.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A tone can sound different depending on whether a syllable is spoken alone or inside a sentence. Sentence intonation and emphasis can affect the pitch you hear.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Does that mean the tone disappears in a sentence?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. The lexical tone remains important, but its surface pitch is shaped by the surrounding speech.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Listen to a native speaker at two speeds. Slow speech helps you notice details; natural speech teaches you how the tone works in conversation.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — six-tone sequence once slowly, a short pause, then twice at a comfortable natural pace.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Should I copy the exact pitch height of the speaker?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Copy the direction and voice quality first. Your comfortable pitch range may differ from the speaker's.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: What if my voice cannot make a very high or low pitch?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: You do not need extreme pitches. The contrast and movement matter more than reaching an impressive high or low note.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us use a listening test. I will name a tone; you recall its movement before saying the syllable.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Ngang: steady and level.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Sắc: rising.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Huyền: falling.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Hỏi: dipping and turning upward, with variation between speakers and contexts.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Ngã: often interrupted or creaky, then rising in Northern speech.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Nặng: short, low and constricted.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I can remember the six labels now. I still need to hear them many times.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is exactly how tone learning works: repeated listening, careful imitation, and meaningful words over time.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: When you meet a new word, do not learn only its consonants and vowel. Learn the tone at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So I should store the whole sound as one memory.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. A word with the wrong tone may be understood as a different word or may be difficult to recognise.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For today's final drill, say each syllable once, pause, then say it again more naturally. Keep the order consistent.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — ma, má, mà, mả, mã, mạ; then repeat in reverse order. Recording not yet supplied.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: The reverse order makes me listen rather than just recite from memory.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. It checks whether you can identify each sound independently.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Finish by saying the six tone names: ngang, sắc, huyền, hỏi, ngã, nặng.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I will practise with the slow model first and then with natural speech.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Accuracy before speed, and relaxed repetition rather than strain. In the next lessons we will keep using tones inside real Vietnamese words and sentences.

title: Vowels and difficult consonants
description: A guided 45–60 minute lesson on Vietnamese vowel contrasts, Northern consonant sounds and final consonants.
teacher_intro: Welcome to Lesson 3. Set aside 45–60 minutes. We will train the Vietnamese vowel letters and several consonant contrasts that English speakers often find unfamiliar. Follow the routine: listen, think, speak aloud, then compare. Use a comfortable voice and a consistent contemporary Northern Vietnamese model. Do not rely on English spelling approximations.
background: Vietnamese has a compact syllable structure. A syllable can contain an initial consonant, a vowel or vowel combination, an optional final consonant and a tone. Vowel letters such as a, ă, â; e, ê; o, ô, ơ; and u, ư are distinct. Marks that change the vowel letter are not tone marks. Initial consonants include digraphs such as ph, th, kh, ng and ngh. In contemporary Hanoi speech, d and gi are commonly pronounced with a z-like sound; r varies by speaker and region and may be similar. tr/ch may be merged or distinguished depending on speaker. Final p, t, c and ch are generally unreleased; final nasals include m, n, ng and nh. Exact realisations vary by context and speaker, so use a consistent native Northern model.
culture: This course uses contemporary Northern Vietnamese with a Hanoi reference accent, while recognising that speakers vary. Spellings remain important even when two initials sound similar in a particular accent. For example, d, gi and r are distinct spellings even where their sounds are close. Regional differences in tr/ch and other consonants are normal. The goal is not to label one regional pronunciation as universally correct; it is to develop a consistent and intelligible model.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Welcome to Lesson 3. Today we train the vowel system and several consonant contrasts that English speakers often find unfamiliar. Allow 45–60 minutes. The goal is not to rush through a list of letters; it is to hear, compare and build accurate syllables.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So today is about making the vowel itself clear before I worry about speaking quickly?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Vietnamese vowels are not interchangeable. A small change in vowel quality can create a different syllable. Keep your jaw, lips and tongue deliberate, and listen to a Northern model.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: First, remember the difference between a letter and a sound. Vietnamese has vowel letters with their own identities: a, ă, â; e, ê; o, ô, ơ; u, ư; and i. The marks on ă, â, ê, ô, ơ and ư are part of the letter, not optional decoration.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So ơ is not just o with an accent added for tone?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. The horn changes the vowel letter. Tone marks are a separate layer. A syllable can have a vowel-shape mark and a tone mark together.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us begin with a and ă. The vowel a is relatively open. The vowel ă is shorter and has a different quality. Do not simply say a and then cut it off at random; learn the contrast as two distinct vowel sounds.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can hear that ă is shorter, but I need to keep its vowel quality distinct too.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Listen to the contrast in isolated syllables: ba and bă. Keep the initial consonant the same so the vowel is the only changing part.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — slow contrast: ba… bă… ba… bă. Repeat with a short pause. Then say the pair at a natural pace.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now compare a and â. The â vowel is more central and shorter than a. Avoid turning â into the English schwa automatically; copy the native model and keep the syllable stable.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So a, ă and â are three different vowel letters, not three spellings of one sound.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Say them in sequence: a, ă, â. Then use the same consonant frame: ba, bă, bâ. The last item is a sound drill, not a vocabulary lesson.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — vowel sequence: a… ă… â…; then ba… bă… bâ… Repeat twice, slowly and clearly.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Next, e and ê. The vowel e is more open; ê is closer and tenser. Keep the lips relaxed and do not add an English glide at the end.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I should not let ê turn into 'ay' as in an English word.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. Vietnamese vowels are generally held as one clear vowel target. Listen: me and mê. Notice the difference in the vowel, not the volume.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — contrast: me… mê… me… mê. Hold each vowel evenly without adding a second sound.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now the rounded back vowels: o, ô and ơ. O is more open, ô is closer and rounded, while ơ is unrounded and more central. The difference between ô and ơ is especially important: do not round your lips for ơ.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So for ô my lips are rounded, but for ơ they are relaxed and unrounded.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Feel the lips rather than exaggerating the jaw. Listen to the three vowels in isolation, then in a simple consonant frame.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — slow: o… ô… ơ…; then bo… bô… bơ. Repeat the sequence twice.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now u and ư. U is a high rounded vowel. For ư, keep the tongue high but relax the rounding: the lips should not form the same small circle.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: U has rounded lips; ư is unrounded. I can use the mirror to check.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a useful technique. Say u, ư, u, ư. Keep the tongue position steady and change the lips.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — contrast: u… ư… u… ư. Then repeat naturally, without adding a glide.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us review the vowel families: a, ă, â; e, ê; o, ô, ơ; u, ư; i. Say each carefully. The point is not to memorise an English approximation; it is to build a reliable listening category for each Vietnamese vowel.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: There are more contrasts than English spelling prepares me for.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. English spelling habits can mislead you. Use the Vietnamese letter and a native recording as your guide.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: We will now look at initial consonants. Vietnamese pinyin-like spellings are not used here; learn the actual Quốc ngữ spelling. For example, ph is pronounced like an English f, not like p plus h.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So phố begins with an f-like sound.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. Listen to phở. Keep the airflow continuous and do not insert a stop before it.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — words: phở, phố, phim. First slowly, then in a natural speaking rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The spelling th represents an aspirated t-like sound. It is not the same as English 'th' in think. Put the tongue at the position for t and release a noticeable puff of air.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So thở starts with an airy t, not the English sound in 'think'.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Compare t and th in a controlled drill. Keep the vowel the same and feel the extra breath after th.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — contrast: ta… tha… ta… tha; then tôi… thôi. Leave a short pause between pairs.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The consonant kh is a friction sound made farther back in the mouth. It is not simply English k. Let air pass through a narrow space without adding a separate vowel.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I should make a soft friction sound, not a hard k followed by h.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Practise slowly with không. Keep the sound comfortable; do not scrape or strain your throat.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — words: không, khỏe, khó. Slow model, then natural repetition.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now the consonants ng and ngh. Both spellings represent the same basic initial sound; ngh is used before certain front vowels according to spelling rules. The sound is like the final sound in English 'sing', but at the beginning of a Vietnamese syllable.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: That feels unusual because English does not normally begin a word with that sound.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Right. Start by making the back-of-the-tongue nasal sound as in 'sing', then move directly into the vowel. Practise nghe and người.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — words: nghe, nghỉ, người, ngon. Model slowly, then at natural pace.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: In contemporary Hanoi speech, the letters d and gi are commonly pronounced with a sound similar to English z. The letter r also has regional and speaker variation; in many Northern models it is pronounced similarly to that z-like sound. Do not assume every region uses the same pronunciation.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So d, gi and r may sound alike in the Northern model, even though they are written differently.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a useful Northern starting point. Learn the spelling separately from the sound, and listen to the speaker you are using as your model.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — words: da, gia, ra; then dạ, già, rã. Read clearly and naturally, without exaggerating the initial consonant.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Some Northern speakers distinguish tr and ch; many contemporary speakers, including in Hanoi, may merge them or realise them very similarly. We will not pretend there is one universal rule. For this course, copy the chosen native model consistently.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should recognise the spellings, but not be surprised if the sounds are close or merged.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Regional and individual variation is part of spoken Vietnamese.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now final consonants. Vietnamese syllables can end in a vowel, a nasal such as m, n, ng or nh, or an unreleased stop such as p, t, c or ch. These final stops are not released with a strong burst of air.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So if a word ends in t, I should not add an extra vowel after it.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. Do not say 'tuh'. Close the syllable cleanly. Listen to mặt and học. The final consonant is brief and unreleased.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — final-stop words: mặt, mắt, học, một. Say each slowly, keeping the final closure short and unreleased.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Compare final m and n. M is made with both lips closed; n uses the tongue at the front of the mouth. Listen to nam and năm: the final consonants are not the same.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I need to notice where the sound is made, not just whether it is nasal.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now compare final n and ng. N is made at the front; ng is made at the back. Practise an and ang as a listening contrast, then copy the full words from the native speaker.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — final nasal contrast: an… ang… an… ang; then ăn… ăng. Keep the vowel and final nasal distinct.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A reminder about syllables: do not insert a vowel after a final consonant, and do not release p, t or c/ch as though you were speaking English. The syllable should finish cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: That means I should avoid adding an English-style extra 'uh' at the end.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Listen to the whole syllable, including its ending. A clear final consonant helps the listener identify the word.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us combine the skills. In người, notice the initial ng, the vowel ươ and the final i. In không, notice kh, ô and final ng. Vietnamese syllables are compact structures; each part matters.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should identify the initial, vowel and ending, then add the tone.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is our practical routine: initial consonant, exact vowel, final consonant, then tone. You do not need to analyse every syllable forever, but it is useful while training.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — careful syllable analysis: người… không… phở… học… khỏe. First separate each word, then repeat the sequence naturally.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Take a short break. When you return, do the listening test without looking at the spelling. Identify the vowel or consonant contrast you hear.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For the first test, listen for the difference between a and ă. Write down which one you hear first, then which one you hear second.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — shuffled vowel test: bă, ba, bâ, bơ, bô, bư, bu. Pause after each item, then repeat in a different order.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Check your notes. If you confused two vowels, practise only that pair for one minute. Do not repeat the entire alphabet without listening carefully.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I confused u and ư because I rounded my lips for both.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Use a mirror. Say u with rounded lips, then ư with unrounded lips. Keep the tongue high in both.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now a consonant test. Listen for ph, th, kh and ng at the beginning of a syllable. Name the sound you hear before reading the word.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — initials: phở, thở, khỏe, nghe. Repeat once slowly and once naturally.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: I can hear that ph is f-like, th is an aspirated t, kh is friction farther back, and ng is nasal.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now practise final consonants. Listen to the end of mặt, nam, an and ang. Do not add a vowel after the final sound.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — endings: mặt… nam… an… ang… học… một. Leave a short pause between items.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Here is a daily five-minute routine. Spend one minute on the vowel family that is hardest for you, one minute on initial consonants, one minute on final consonants, one minute listening without text, and one minute repeating complete words.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Should I practise every sound at maximum volume so I can feel it?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. Use a comfortable speaking voice. Accuracy comes from placement and listening, not force. Stop if your throat feels strained.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Final challenge. Without looking, name the vowel contrasts a/ă/â, e/ê, o/ô/ơ and u/ư. Then explain the difference between ph, th, kh and ng. Finally, say người, không, phở and học carefully.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — final review: a, ă, â; e, ê; o, ô, ơ; u, ư; phở, thở, không, nghe, người, học. Slow model followed by natural-speed repetition.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: You have completed Lesson 3. The most important habit is to hear the exact sound rather than guess from English spelling. In Lesson 4 we will use these pronunciation skills in your first greetings. Keep your listening routine short and regular.

Th is an aspirated t-like sound, not the English th in think.

title: Your first greetings
description: Build a natural first exchange: hello, how are you, a response, returning the question and goodbye.
teacher_intro: Welcome to Lesson 4. We will construct your first Northern Vietnamese greeting exchange one small piece at a time. Think before speaking, say the Vietnamese aloud, then compare. Allow 45–60 minutes, including the listening and speaking drills.
background: Vietnamese greetings are built around social relationships. Xin chào is a polite, broadly understood greeting. In everyday speech, chào is often followed by an address term such as anh, chị, em, cô or chú. A simple learner question is bạn khỏe không? with the response tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn? returns the question. Mình is common in friendly peer conversation, while tôi is relatively neutral or formal. These pronouns and address terms are not interchangeable in every relationship.
culture: A Vietnamese greeting is more than a literal translation of hello. The choice of address term can signal age, familiarity, respect and relationship. Do not guess that every adult man is anh or every adult woman is chị; context and the other person’s preference matter. Xin chào is useful and polite, but everyday speakers may use a shorter chào plus an appropriate address term. Chào buổi sáng is understandable, though it can sound more like a set phrase than the most common everyday greeting.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Welcome to Lesson 4. Today we will build a first greeting exchange in contemporary Northern Vietnamese. You will learn how to say hello, ask how someone is, answer naturally, return the question and say goodbye. Work slowly: listen, think, speak aloud, then compare.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Are we going to memorise a whole conversation, or build it piece by piece?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Piece by piece. First we make a greeting. Then we add a question. Then we make a response and pass the question back. By the end, you will be able to build the exchange without reading it.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The phrase xin chào is a polite, widely understood way to say hello. Listen to the two syllables: xin… chào. Keep them distinct and give chào its rising tone.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Xin chào.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now say it again as one natural greeting, not as two isolated vocabulary items.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — Northern Hanoi model: xin chào… xin chào. First slowly with a pause between syllables, then naturally as a greeting. Repeat twice.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: You can also hear chào used without xin. Chào is the core greeting. In everyday Vietnamese, the greeting often includes a form of address, such as chào anh or chào chị. The right form depends on the relationship.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So xin chào is a safe polite phrase, but people often greet one another with a relationship word.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. For now, learn xin chào as your reliable starting point. We will practise address terms carefully rather than guessing someone’s age or relationship.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now let us ask how someone is. A simple learner pattern is bạn khỏe không? Build it in three parts: bạn… khỏe… không?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn khỏe không?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. The word không at the end marks a yes-or-no question in this pattern. Do not turn the whole sentence into an English-style rising question automatically. Follow the Northern recording for the natural contour.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — question: bạn khỏe không? Slow model, pause, repeat; then natural conversational version. Repeat three times.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Notice bạn. It can work when speaking to a peer or someone you address as bạn, but it is not a universal word for every person. Vietnamese commonly uses relationship-sensitive address terms.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Could I say anh khỏe không?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes, if anh is the appropriate way to address that man in the relationship. Chị is commonly used for a woman addressed as an older sister or adult woman. The choice is social, not just grammatical.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For this first practice, keep bạn khỏe không? as our simple classroom pattern. Later, we will learn to choose address terms with more confidence.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now answer. Tôi khỏe means I am well. Say it in two parts: tôi… khỏe.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi khỏe.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Tôi is a relatively neutral or formal first-person pronoun. In everyday conversation, speakers often use other pronouns depending on the relationship. We are using tôi to make the first pattern clear.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — response: tôi khỏe. Slow model, then natural pace. Keep the hỏi tone in khỏe clear, without exaggerating it.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us make the response a little warmer: tôi khỏe, cảm ơn — I am well, thank you. You already know that cảm ơn means thank you. Join the chunks smoothly.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. Now we can return the question with còn bạn? This means and you? or what about you? Listen: còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — phrase: còn bạn? Model slowly, then naturally. Repeat after a short pause.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Put the response and return question together: tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a complete conversational turn. Notice that the question comes back to the other person, so the exchange feels balanced.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us build the whole conversation. I say xin chào. You answer xin chào. I ask bạn khỏe không? You answer tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Xin chào. Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. We will make it more natural with two speakers. Listen first; do not speak over the model.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — mini-dialogue, two native voices: A: Xin chào! B: Xin chào! A: Bạn khỏe không? B: Mình khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn? A: Mình cũng khỏe, cảm ơn. Natural Hanoi conversational pace, then repeat slowly.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: You heard mình khỏe. Mình is a friendly first-person pronoun often used among peers or in familiar conversation. It can also appear in reciprocal expressions. For our formal-clear classroom pattern, tôi khỏe is still useful.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So tôi is a little more neutral or formal, while mình can sound friendlier with someone familiar.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a helpful first approximation. Pronoun choice depends on relationship and context, so do not treat either word as a universal replacement.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now add cũng, meaning also or too. Tôi cũng khỏe means I am well too. Listen: tôi… cũng… khỏe.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi cũng khỏe.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now answer the question: tôi cũng khỏe, cảm ơn. Keep cũng as its own syllable and preserve its tone.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — contrast and phrase: khỏe… cũng khỏe… tôi cũng khỏe, cảm ơn. Slow, then natural.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Sometimes a person may say bình thường, meaning normal or so-so, depending on tone and context. It is a useful response, but today do not overcomplicate the first exchange. Your core answer is tôi khỏe, cảm ơn.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: If I am not especially well, can I say không khỏe?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Không khỏe means not well. You can say tôi không khỏe — I am not well. We will practise it as an extra pattern, not as the centre of today’s lesson.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — extra response: tôi không khỏe. Say it gently and naturally; do not sound overly dramatic.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us practise a few greetings for different situations. Chào anh is hello to someone you appropriately address as anh. Chào chị is hello to someone you appropriately address as chị. Listen to the difference in the address word.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Chào anh. Chào chị.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Do not select anh or chị only from a quick guess. Age, relationship, setting and the other person’s preference matter. When unsure, listen to how people introduce themselves or how others address them.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For a group, chào mọi người means hello everyone. Mọi người refers to everyone or everybody. This is useful when entering a room or addressing a group.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Chào mọi người!

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — group greeting: chào mọi người. Warm, friendly Northern delivery, first slowly and then at natural pace.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: You may also hear chào buổi sáng for good morning. It is understandable and correct, though in everyday conversation a simple chào with the right address term is often more natural. Learn it as a useful phrase, not as the only way to greet someone in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Chào buổi sáng.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now let us leave a conversation. Tạm biệt means goodbye. Say the two syllables carefully: tạm… biệt.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tạm biệt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A common friendly way to say bye is bye, borrowed from English, but we will use tạm biệt as our clear Vietnamese phrase. You may also hear chào nhé as a friendly leave-taking, depending on the situation.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — leave-taking: tạm biệt… chào nhé. Slow model, then natural conversational pace. Keep the final consonants neat.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now listen to the difference between greeting someone and leaving them. Xin chào opens the interaction. Tạm biệt closes it. Chào can also be used in both directions when paired with an appropriate address term or context.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should not assume that every English hello or goodbye maps to only one Vietnamese word.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Learn the phrase as it is used in context, not as a one-word translation.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us do a substitution drill. I say bạn khỏe không? You answer tôi khỏe. Then return the question: còn bạn? Ready?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi khỏe. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now add cảm ơn.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now change tôi to mình for a friendly peer conversation.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Mình khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now answer that question with tôi cũng khỏe.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi cũng khỏe, cảm ơn.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. You have built a two-way exchange from small pieces.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Take a short break. When you return, listen to the native recording without looking at the text. Identify the greeting, the question, the answer and the goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — listening passage, natural speed: A: Xin chào! B: Chào bạn! A: Bạn khỏe không? B: Mình khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn? A: Mình cũng khỏe. Cảm ơn nhé. B: Tạm biệt! A: Chào nhé! Pause for the learner to identify each turn, then repeat slowly.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let us check the meaning. Which phrase opened the conversation?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Xin chào.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Which phrase asked how the other person was?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn khỏe không?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Which phrase returned the question?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: And which phrase ended the conversation?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tạm biệt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now practise pronunciation using what you learned in Lessons 1 to 3. In khỏe, listen for the vowel and the hỏi tone. In bạn, keep the final n closed cleanly. In cảm ơn, keep the two vowel qualities distinct and do not add an extra vowel after the final consonant.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — sound focus: bạn… khỏe… không… cảm ơn… tạm biệt. First slow, with a brief pause between words; then repeat in phrases.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Do not exaggerate tones or speak unnaturally slowly forever. Slow practice is for accuracy. Once the syllables are clear, join them at a comfortable conversational speed.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I should keep the tones clear but make the whole greeting sound friendly, not like a spelling test.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. A greeting is also a social action. A warm expression, suitable eye contact and an appropriate form of address help the words fit the situation.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Final challenge. Without looking, greet someone, ask how they are, say that you are well and thank them, return the question, say that you are well too, then say goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Xin chào. Bạn khỏe không? Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn? Tôi cũng khỏe. Tạm biệt!

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Well done. You have completed Lesson 4. You can now build a simple greeting exchange. In Lesson 5 we will introduce yourself and say your name. Keep practising this conversation until you can produce it without reading.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording script — final model conversation: Xin chào! Bạn khỏe không? Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn bạn? Tôi cũng khỏe, cảm ơn. Tạm biệt! Record in a clear contemporary Northern Hanoi voice, with natural rhythm, then a slower learner version.

title: Introducing yourself
description: Build a natural personal introduction: your name, nationality, country of origin and where you live. Ask another person the same questions.
teacher_intro: Welcome to Lesson 5. Today you will introduce yourself in Northern Vietnamese. By the end, you will be able to say your name, say where you come from, identify your nationality, explain where you live now, and ask another person those questions. We will build each sentence from small pieces. Do not simply read the answer: pause, construct it aloud, then compare. Use the neutral beginner pronoun tôi for yourself and bạn for a peer. In real conversation, Vietnamese pronouns and forms of address depend on age, relationship and setting; we will develop those choices in later lessons.
background: Vietnamese introductions are built from reusable sentence patterns. Tên tôi là… and Tôi tên là… both mean 'My name is…' / 'I am called…'. Tôi đến từ… means 'I come from…'. Tôi là người… identifies nationality or origin by saying 'I am a … person'. Tôi sống ở… means 'I live in…'. To ask where someone comes from, use Bạn đến từ đâu?; đâu means 'where'. To ask where someone lives, use Bạn sống ở đâu? The word người means 'person'. The country name Tanzania can be used as a proper name; Úc is the usual Vietnamese name for Australia. The connector nhưng means 'but'. Notice that Vietnamese does not need an equivalent of English 'am' in every sentence: tôi sống ở Úc is complete without là.
culture: A first introduction is usually brief. You do not need to give your full biography immediately. Start with a greeting and name, then add where you are from or where you live if it is relevant. Vietnamese speakers may ask quê bạn ở đâu? ('Where is your home place?') or quê quán to ask about family/home origins; this is not always the same as asking which country you come from. Bạn is a useful classroom pronoun between peers, but it is not a universal form of address for every real-life relationship. In later lessons you will practise choosing anh, chị, em and other kinship-based pronouns. When saying you live in Australia, say sống ở Úc. Country names are proper names, and pronunciation may be adapted naturally by Vietnamese speakers.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's begin with a name. In Vietnamese, tên means 'name'. To say 'My name is…', one natural pattern is tên tôi là…

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tên tôi là Linh.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Tên tôi là Linh: literally, 'name – I – is – Linh'. Now replace Linh with your own name. Pause and say the complete sentence.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tên tôi là Minh.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: There is another common order: tôi tên là… Both tên tôi là… and tôi tên là… are used. For this lesson, practise both, but keep one pattern at a time until it feels easy.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi tên là Anna.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now ask another person their name. Bạn means 'you' in this simple peer-to-peer practice. Gì means 'what'. Put the pieces together: bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Notice that gì stays at the end of this question. Vietnamese often places a question word where the answer would appear.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt: tên tôi là…; tôi tên là…; bạn tên là gì? First slow and clearly, then at natural Hanoi conversational speed. Audio recording not supplied yet.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's practise the exchange. I ask: bạn tên là gì? You answer with your own name. Pause now.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tên tôi là David.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. You can also add a polite greeting before the question: xin chào. Say the two sentences together.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Xin chào. Bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now we will say where a person comes from. The small word đến means 'come/arrive'. Từ means 'from'. Together, đến từ means 'come from'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Đến từ.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: To say 'I come from Tanzania', begin with tôi, then đến từ, then the country name. Build it before the student answers.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi đến từ Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. Keep the structure in this order: tôi + đến từ + place. Now try 'I come from Australia'. Remember the Vietnamese country name Úc.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi đến từ Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Úc is the usual Vietnamese name for Australia. Now ask 'Where do you come from?' Keep the same sentence and replace the person and place with a question word: đâu means 'where'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn đến từ đâu?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. Bạn đến từ đâu? Do not move đâu to the beginning. It occupies the place where the country name would go.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt: tôi đến từ Tanzania; tôi đến từ Úc; bạn đến từ đâu? Contrast the tones and syllable rhythm. Audio recording not supplied yet.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now let's distinguish coming from a country and being a person of that nationality. Người means 'person'. To say 'I am Tanzanian', say tôi là người Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi là người Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Very good. Here là is needed to identify what kind of person you are: tôi là người… Now say 'I am Australian'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi là người Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Compare the two patterns: tôi đến từ Tanzania means 'I come from Tanzania'; tôi là người Tanzania means 'I am Tanzanian'. They are related, but they do not have exactly the same structure.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So người is the word that makes the nationality pattern?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Người means person. Keep it in the sentence when you use this pattern.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now ask someone their nationality: bạn là người nước nào? Nước means country, and nào means which. The question means 'Which country are you from / what nationality are you?'

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn là người nước nào?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is a useful question, though in a first conversation bạn đến từ đâu? is often simpler. Practise both and notice the difference in meaning.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt: tôi là người Tanzania; tôi là người Úc; bạn là người nước nào? Slow repetition then natural-speed question/answer. Audio recording not supplied yet.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now say where you live. Sống means 'live'. Ở means 'in' or 'at' for a location. Start with tôi, then sống ở, then the place.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Tôi sống ở Úc means 'I live in Australia'. There is no need to add là. Say 'I live in Tanzania'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi sống ở Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now ask someone where they live. Keep sống ở and replace the location with đâu.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn sống ở đâu?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Compare the two questions: bạn đến từ đâu? asks where someone comes from; bạn sống ở đâu? asks where they live now. They may have different answers.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can come from Tanzania but live in Australia.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Let's build that complete idea in Vietnamese. First say 'I am Tanzanian': tôi là người Tanzania. Then we need 'but'. The word nhưng means 'but'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Nhưng.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: After nhưng, say 'I live in Australia': tôi sống ở Úc. Join the two parts. You may repeat tôi after nhưng to make the sentence clear.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi là người Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. This is a complete and natural introduction detail: 'I am Tanzanian, but I live in Australia.' You can also say tôi đến từ Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc — 'I come from Tanzania, but I live in Australia'.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi đến từ Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Both are useful. The first states nationality; the second states country of origin. Choose the one that expresses what you mean.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt: tôi là người Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc; tôi đến từ Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc. Read with a natural pause around nhưng. Audio recording not supplied yet.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's make a short conversation. Listen to the first speaker, then pause and answer as yourself.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Xin chào. Bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Xin chào. Tên tôi là Linh. Còn bạn?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Còn bạn? means 'And you?' or 'What about you?' It is a very useful way to return a question. Now answer with your name.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi tên là Jeremiah.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now one person asks where the other comes from.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn đến từ đâu?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi đến từ Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now ask where the person lives. Notice that this is a different question.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn sống ở đâu?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now combine nationality and residence in one longer answer.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi là người Tanzania, nhưng tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: À, hay quá!

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: À is a conversational response like 'Oh'. Hay quá means 'That's great!' We will study reactions and natural responses in a later lesson. For now, recognise the expression.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A quick note about pronouns. We are using tôi and bạn as a clear classroom pair. In real Vietnamese, speakers often choose pronouns according to relative age and relationship. You might hear anh, chị, em, cô or chú instead. Do not try to guess these forms yet; use tôi and bạn for today's controlled practice.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So the grammar pattern stays the same, but the pronoun can change?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. The sentence frame remains useful. Later we will practise choosing the right form of address for the person you are speaking to.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's review the four main patterns. My name is…: tên tôi là… I come from…: tôi đến từ… I am a … person: tôi là người… I live in…: tôi sống ở… Say each one aloud with your own details.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tên tôi là Jeremiah.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi đến từ Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi là người Tanzania.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi sống ở Úc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now ask the matching questions: what is your name; where do you come from; what nationality are you; where do you live? Pause after each English prompt and build the Vietnamese question.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn tên là gì?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn đến từ đâu?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn là người nước nào?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn sống ở đâu?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
